Good timing — I've now read all the relevant files. Here's my thinking on each area:

---

## Assets & Entities

The current tab does a lot — physical components, world entities, AI image generation, property panels, entity-to-rule linking — but it all flows linearly top-to-bottom without much visual hierarchy. Some ideas:

- **Split-panel layout**: Left column is a collapsible entity/asset browser (grouped by type, searchable), right panel shows the full detail view for the selected item — similar to how a code editor or Finder works. Right now editing and browsing fight for the same vertical space.
- **Promoted property panel**: Entity properties (`EntityProperty`) are powerful but feel buried. A dedicated "Stats & Attributes" section within each entity detail — similar to how Assets already has a multi-field status/kind system — would make this more visible.
- **Component map**: A visual "canvas" view (toggle from list view) showing all components as cards laid out by category, so you can see the full component inventory at a glance without scrolling.
- **Cross-links surfaced on the card**: Each entity card could show a small inline "Linked rules: 2, Linked assets: 1" count that's clickable, rather than having to expand and scroll. Entity-to-rule linking exists in the data layer but isn't prominent in the UI.

---

## Rules — Markdown / Rulebook View

Your instinct is right — individual sandbox cards are great for iteration but terrible for understanding how rules *fit together* as a system. Ideas:

- **Dual-mode toggle**: a "Sandbox" mode (current card view, good for AI iteration and conflict checking) and a **"Rulebook" mode** — a live Markdown document that assembles rules into sections by category with proper headings, paragraph flow, and numbered clauses.
- **Inline MD editor**: The Rulebook view would be an actual editable Markdown textarea (rendered with something like `react-markdown` + `remark`) — so rules can have headers like `## 3. Combat` with sub-rules listed below them. Each section maps to a category.
- **Auto-generated table of contents**: Derived from category groupings, so the designer can see the full structure at a glance — "does my rulebook have gaps?"
- **Completeness scoring**: A small sidebar metric — "Rules cover: Movement ✓, Combat ✓, Win Conditions ✗, Setup ✗" — using AI to flag structural holes rather than just individual card conflicts.
- **Export-ready**: The MD view doubles as the export source for the Exports tab, so the rules actually look like a document someone could hand to a playtester.

---

## Players Tab

Compared to Assets & Entities — which has subtypes, custom properties, status tracking, AI image generation, and rule linking — Players is relatively shallow: name, type, role, description, strategy. Ideas to bring it up to parity:

- **Stat blocks**: A key-value property system (just like `EntityProperty` for Entities) — HP, Speed, Attack, Defense, special attributes. Could be freeform or templated by player type.
- **Linked abilities and factions**: Players currently have no connection to the `Ability` or `Faction` entity types. A small linked-entities row on the player card (matching the LinkedEntitiesBar pattern from Rules) would tie the data model together.
- **Relationship map**: A small visual diagram showing "Character A is allied with NPC B, opposed to Enemy C" — especially useful for narrative-heavy games. Could be a simple force-directed graph.
- **Playbook section**: Expand "Strategy" into a richer section — maybe AI-generated decision trees, encounter behaviors, or loot tables for enemies/bosses.
- **Portrait/art slot**: The same AI image generation pipeline that Assets uses (component art) could be available here for character portraits.

---

## Research Tab

Currently a flat card grid — title, URL, notes, tags. It works but doesn't connect research back to the design. Ideas:

- **Category system** replacing free-form tags: "Mechanical Inspiration", "Theme Reference", "Competitor Analysis", "Playtest Feedback", "Market Research" — with color-coded lanes like the Rules categories.
- **Link research to specific rules or entities**: A "inspired by" trail — clicking a rule could show which research items influenced it, and vice versa. This makes the design reasoning traceable.
- **AI Synthesis button**: Takes all tagged research items and asks the AI "what patterns are emerging here? What design direction is implied?" — a higher-level insight pass rather than per-card enhancement.
- **Board / kanban view**: Research items as swimlane columns by category rather than a flat grid — easier to spot imbalances (e.g. "all my research is mechanical, nothing thematic").
- **Timestamps and design phase annotations**: Show when each item was added relative to the current design phase, so you can see how research evolved alongside the project.

---

## Board Game Shelf (Reference Games)

Currently lives in **Overview** as the "Reference games" card. The right new home is **Research** — semantically, reference games ARE a form of research (competitor/inspiration analysis). 

In Research it could get its own promoted section at the top: a dedicated "Reference Shelf" block, visually distinct from individual sources (maybe even a card-style shelf layout with box-art placeholders), with the "borrowing / avoiding" fields intact. This would also let the Research tab auto-query BGG or Wikipedia for basic info when a game name is entered — title, year, mechanic tags — saving the designer from manually describing it.

---

**Short version**: Rules needs a document-layer on top of the sandbox, Players needs the same depth as Assets, Research needs categories + cross-links, the shelf moves there naturally, and Assets benefits most from a split-panel detail view. Want me to start on any of these?

Now I have a complete picture. Here's my thinking across all of these:

---

## Spreadsheet View for Entities

The current `EntityProperties` panel (`assets-entities.tsx:1955`) already has a table-like grid but it only shows *one entity's properties at a time* — one row per property. The problem is when you have 60 cards in a deck or 100 tiles in Azul's bag, you need the inverse: **one row per entity, one column per property**.

What I'd add:

- **Toggle between Card view and Sheet view** at the top of EntitiesView. Sheet view renders all entities as a spreadsheet — rows are entities, columns are: Name, Type, Subtype, and then every `EntityProperty` key that exists across that entity type.
- **Inline cell editing** — click a cell, edit in place, Tab to next. No dialog required.
- **Bulk row add** — "+ Add 10 rows" that creates blank entity stubs you fill in. Critical for Skip-Bo (144 cards) or Azul (100 tiles).
- **CSV import/export** — paste from Google Sheets / Excel directly. This is a huge workflow win for designers who already have their card list in a spreadsheet.
- **Column pinning** — pin Name, freeze the left column while scrolling right through custom properties.
- **Computed/formula columns** — read-only columns derived from others. For a combat game: `Power = Attack + Defense`. These don't need to be stored, just displayed.

The key data model gap: right now entities don't have a `quantity` field — assets do, but entities don't. For Azul's tiles, the entity IS the tile type ("Blue Tile") and quantity belongs on it (20). That needs to be a first-class entity field, not just an asset field.

---

## Card Text & Deck Contents

This is the biggest gap. When you define a Deck entity, there's no place to define what's *inside* it. The Gamma prompt builder (`buildDeckPrompt`) already knows this structure exists conceptually but the data layer and UI don't surface it.

What I'd build:

- **Deck → Cards parent/child relationship**: When you expand a Deck entity in the Sheet view, it shows its child Card entities as nested rows. A "Cards in this deck" expandable section in the card view too.
- **Card Studio panel**: Click into a Deck → a dedicated panel opens showing all cards in the deck as a spreadsheet. Columns: Name, Subtype, Cost/Value, Effect Text, Flavor Text, Quantity in Deck, Art Description. This maps exactly to what a physical card would need.
- **AI batch generation for card text**: A text prompt like *"Generate 20 action cards for a dungeon-crawl deck — mix attack, defense, and event cards"* → AI fills in the full spreadsheet with names, effects, and flavor text. More powerful than the current one-at-a-time approach.
- **Card text templates per subtype**: Each subtype (Action, Item, Spell, Event) has a different field schema. An Action card has "Cost + Effect"; an Event card has "Trigger + Duration + Effect". Templates enforce consistent structure across the deck.
- **Card preview panel**: Side panel showing a rough layout of how the text would sit on the card — title bar, effect box, flavor text in italics — not fully rendered art but enough to catch "the text is too long for this card".
- **Quantity-aware totals**: Bottom of deck spreadsheet shows total card count, quantity-weighted (if you have 3 copies of "Goblin Attack" it counts as 3, not 1).

---

## Broadening Beyond Card/Deck Games

The current framing is card-game-centric even though the component types theoretically support everything. Here's how I'd think about each:

**Azul (tile drafting, pattern placement)**
- Components: Tile (5 color variants × 20 = 100), Factory display board (Player board), Scoring track (Board), Center pool (abstract zone)
- What's missing: **Color-variant system** — Blue Tile and Yellow Tile are the same entity type but different colors with exact quantities. Right now you'd have to make 5 separate Token/Tile entities and manually set quantity to 20 each. A "Variant set" feature on a component type (name: "Azul Tile", variants: Blue/Yellow/Red/Black/White, quantity each: 20) would make this natural.
- The pattern grid (wall) on the player board needs a **grid designer tool** — a visual N×N grid where you can mark which cell takes which color. That's specific to Azul-style games.

**Heat: Pedal to the Metal (racing, gear+deck management)**
- Components: Speed cards (deck, values 1-6), Heat cards (deck), Upgrade cards, Track tiles (modular hex/curve pieces), Dashboard, Gear marker, Car token
- What's missing: **Modular track/tile sequencer** — a tool to lay out tile pieces in order to form a circuit. Think of it as a tile editor where tiles chain together with connection points. Also **numeric card values** as a first-class property (not just subtype) so the deck statistics (avg speed, heat distribution) can be calculated.

**Pirate's Dice / Liar's Dice (dice + bluffing)**
- Components: 5 dice per player, cups
- Extremely component-light. What matters is the **die face designer** — custom dice where you define what's on each of the 6 faces, with icons or values. Also a **probability table** in the Simulator: given N dice, what's the probability of exactly K sixes?
- The current Die type exists as an entity but has no face definition tool.

**Skip-Bo (card sequencing, hand management)**
- Components: 162 cards (numbers 1–12, plus 18 Skip-Bo wild cards), discard piles, building piles
- Almost entirely handled by the spreadsheet view — a numbered card set is just rows in a table. The missing piece is **pile/zone modeling**: modeling game zones (draw pile, discard pile, building piles, stockpile, hand) as first-class design concepts, not just implied by the rules text. A "Zone Map" component — named zones with their properties (shared/private, face-up/face-down, max size) — would serve Skip-Bo, Solitaire, and any hand-management game.

**Universal needs across all these:**
- Remove the assumption that every game has cards. A project tagged as "Tile Placement" shouldn't show Deck-specific tools prominently.
- Game type tagging at project creation should pre-configure which entity types, tools, and templates are surfaced.
- "Zone modeling" (draw pile, bag, discard, board areas) as a component concept.
- A **component manifest / bill of materials** view — total component count across the entire game with quantities. Azul's reads: 100 tiles, 5 factory boards, 1 center display, 4 player boards, 1 scoring track, 1 bag. This is also the thing you hand to a manufacturer.

---

## Monopoly as the Training / Reference Game

This is exactly the right instinct. Monopoly is universally known, component-rich, and mechanically diverse — it's the best possible worked example.

**How Monopoly maps to GameForge's data model:**

| GameForge Type | Monopoly Component |
|---|---|
| Board | The main 40-space board |
| Tile | Individual board spaces (Go, Jail, Free Parking, Properties) |
| Card | Chance cards (16), Community Chest cards (16) |
| Deck | Chance deck, Community Chest deck |
| Token (Meeple) | Player tokens (top hat, car, dog…) |
| Token (Resource) | Money — $1, $5, $10, $20, $50, $100, $500 denominations |
| Token | Houses (32), Hotels (12) |
| Die | 2 standard d6 |
| Faction | Color groups (Brown, Light Blue, Pink, Orange, Red, Yellow, Green, Dark Blue) |
| Resource | Individual property deed cards |
| Entity Property | Purchase price, rent tiers ×6, mortgage value, build cost |

That's every single entity type used, which is why it's the perfect training example.

**What I'd build around this:**

- A **"Demo: Monopoly"** pre-built project that ships with the app — all entities defined, key rules written, turn structure set. Users can explore a real game as a reference instead of building from scratch. This also doubles as a stress test of every feature.
- The **Learn section** (which I saw references `design-101.tsx`) should have a dedicated "Deconstruct a game" module using Monopoly — "here's every decision Hasbro made and why, mapped to GameForge concepts."
- The AI chat should have Monopoly in its system context when the user hasn't defined their own reference games yet — so early suggestions are grounded in something concrete.
- A **"Model a game you know"** onboarding path: pick Monopoly (or Catan, or Chess) → see how it's structured → use that as the starting point for your own design.

---

## What Else I'd Add

A few more ideas that fall out of all this:

**Component Bill of Materials (BOM) view** — a manufacturing-focused table: every component, its type, quantity, dimensions, and a rough unit-cost tier (cheap: dice/tokens, medium: cards, expensive: custom boards). For any designer thinking about publishing, "how much will this cost to make 1000 copies?" is an early critical question. This could live in the Exports tab.

**Zone Map** — as mentioned above, a named-zone system (Draw Pile, Discard, Hand, Board Zone A, Bag) with properties (public/private, ordered/unordered, face-up/face-down, capacity). This makes hand-management, drafting, and bag-building games model naturally without forcing everything into deck metaphors.

**Die Face Designer** — a simple die face editor: 6 faces, each with a value or icon. Used for custom dice in games like King of Tokyo, Roll for the Galaxy, or any game with custom dice mechanics. Feeds directly into the Simulator's probability calculations.

**Blind Playtest Export** — a read-only, shareable web link or PDF of just the rules and component list. No editor UI, no AI panels — just what a playtester needs. This is distinct from the current Exports tab which feels more asset-download focused.

**Complexity Score** — a real-time estimate derived from rule count, entity count, property depth, player count range, and turn phase count — output as a 1–5 complexity tier (BGG scale equivalent) with a breakdown of which factors are driving it up. Useful for positioning your game in the market.

**Quick Reference Card generator** — a 2-sided half-page player aid, auto-generated from rules + turn structure. Every hobbyist-published game needs one. Could be the first thing coming out of the Exports tab for any game type.

---

**Short version**: the spreadsheet view and deck card studio are the highest-value near-term additions. Monopoly as a demo project is a cheap, high-leverage feature that makes every other tool immediately understandable. The broadening to non-card games mostly requires zone modeling, component variant/quantity system, and removing card-first assumptions from the UI. Want to start implementing any of these?
